stories.headline: Senate control remains toss-up as key races tighten

claims.text: Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority.
Republicans need to retain 50 seats to keep control, since Vice President JD Vance casts tie-breaking votes.
Fox News' final Power Rankings rate overall Senate control a toss-up.
Democrats favored in 48 seats and Republicans favored in 47 according to Fox News' final Power Rankings.

A Suffolk University poll released Wednesday shows Democrat Sherrod Brown leading Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, 47% to 44%, with a margin of error of ±4.4 points, 4% undecided and 3% backing another candidate.
A Siena College/New York Times poll shows Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., tied with Democrat Annie Andrews at 48% each, with 3% undecided and under 1% for another candidate.

Fox News shifted its rating on three races: Ohio moved from toss-up to Lean Democrat, South Carolina moved from Likely Republican to Lean Republican, and Mississippi moved from Solid Republican to Likely Republican.
Other races rated toss-up in the Power Rankings include Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Texas and Michigan.
New Hampshire and Minnesota are rated Lean Democrat.
Kansas and South Carolina are rated Lean Republican.

Sen. Darline Graham was appointed in July to the South Carolina seat following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Control of the Senate hinges on a small number of competitive races, several of which are in states that President Trump carried in 2024.
Historically, the party controlling the White House tends to lose congressional seats in midterm years.
Fox News' reporting notes that inflation, an unpopular conflict involving Iran, and Trump's approval ratings form the backdrop against which Republicans are defending their majority.

Because Vice President Vance can break a 50-50 tie, Republicans have a one-seat cushion in the chamber, needing only 50 seats to retain control while Democrats must win enough seats outright to overcome that advantage.

stories.headline: Supreme Court upholds Trump administration's ability to block immigration judges' closures

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: In 2024, the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), a DOJ component under the Biden administration, adopted a rule formally allowing immigration judges to use 'administrative closure' to temporarily suspend certain deportation proceedings, including when migrants sought relief such as asylum through USCIS.

In June, Texas sued the federal government in Wichita Falls, Texas, with the case assigned to Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor, a George W. Bush appointee, arguing the EOIR lacked legal authority to adopt the administrative-closure rule.
The same day the suit was filed, the DOJ agreed with Texas and asked O'Connor to vacate the rule and bar similar future rules; O'Connor granted that request that day, entering a consent judgment.

On Aug. 7, Baltimore, New Haven, Columbus, and the advocacy group Centro Legal de la Raza moved to intervene to defend the rule on appeal, arguing elimination of the rule could cost them tax revenue through deportations; O'Connor denied the motion for lack of legal standing.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit rejected the challengers' request to block the consent judgment while their appeal proceeded.
On Oct. 9, the challengers asked the Supreme Court to pause O'Connor's judgment, alleging 'egregious collusion' between Texas and the DOJ in reaching the consent agreement.

On Oct. 27, 2026, the Supreme Court denied the challengers' request in an unsigned order with no noted dissents, leaving in place the lower court ruling that eliminated the administrative-closure rule.
The Biden-era DOJ formalized that practice in 2024.
Texas challenged it as exceeding EOIR's statutory authority.
The Trump-era DOJ chose not to defend the rule, instead agreeing with Texas to have it vacated via a consent judgment issued the same day the case was filed.

The core legal question that reached the Supreme Court was not whether the rule itself was lawful, but whether outside parties—three cities and an immigrant-legal-services group—had the legal standing to intervene and keep defending the rule on appeal after the original defendant (DOJ) stopped contesting it.

By declining to intervene, the Supreme Court left intact both the lower court's vacatur of the rule and its finding that the cities lacked standing, without ruling on the broader merits of the collusion allegations.

With the administrative-closure rule vacated and the Supreme Court declining to intervene, immigration judges will no longer have that mechanism to pause certain deportation proceedings, potentially affecting migrants pursuing parallel relief like asylum claims.

stories.headline: At least 68 killed in Spanish high-speed train crash
body: At least 68 people were killed when a high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped on the tracks in central Spain on Wednesday morning, in the country's second deadly high-speed rail collision this year. The crash occurred just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz in Toledo province, about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid, and knocked two carriages off the track and down an embankment, scattering debris across a gravel slope. Train operator Adif said a state-owned Renfe train collided with a private Iryo train, which covered the Madrid to Seville route. The Iryo train was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe train had 397 passengers, according to Castilla-La Mancha regional government spokesperson Esther Padilla. A passenger on the Renfe train told broadcaster TVE: "We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact. The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."

Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called an "inexplicable" decision by a central command centre after a computer failure. He said the security system on a 63km (39-mile) stretch stopped working at 8:30 a.m., causing all trains on that stretch to stop, including the six moving trains. The control centre then ordered the Renfe train to start moving again without any speed restrictions, even though a stop signal was still active on the line. Puente said the train should never have been allowed to proceed, and if it had, it should have been told to go at reduced speed. He said engineers were not to blame, and investigators were still studying how fast the train was travelling, but it could have been at up to 200 kph (124 mph). "I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," he said.

Rescue crews were focusing on extracting survivors and bodies from the two most damaged carriages, Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said. At least 80 people were being treated for injuries, with 50 reported in serious condition and 15 in critical condition. Hospitals in the area suspended planned surgeries, and a Madrid blood transfusion centre appealed for urgent donations. A military emergency brigade, firefighters, police, ambulances and medical helicopters were deployed to the rural site, while uninjured survivors were put on buses. The nearby town of Urda prepared a sports pavilion to receive the injured.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who cancelled all public engagements including election campaigning, said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and promised a thorough investigation. "The pain is immense," he said at the crash site. "We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light. If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness." King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia said they were "deeply saddened and concerned," and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, "My heart goes out to the victims' families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you." Spain's football federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for Wednesday, with Barcelona, Real Madrid and other clubs expressing condolences.

The crash is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year. In January, 46 people were killed in southern Spain when an Iryo train jumped the track and struck an oncoming Renfe train. That was the deadliest rail accident in Spain since 2013, when 80 people died in a derailment. Until this year, no fatal crash had occurred on Spain's dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992, a source of national pride. Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail, laying about 3,900km (2,400 miles) of track, second only to China's 45,000km, according to the International Union of Railways. Rail service between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia was suspended, and all train traffic on the affected line was halted.

Iryo, an Italian-owned company that began operating in Spain in 2022, said it had "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities." A spokesperson for Spain's train workers' union suggested that privatisation had increased use of the network and placed extra strain on infrastructure. "We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," said Joan Rodríguez. "I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind." The government said it was still determining the exact origin of the tragedy.

stories.headline: No clear winner in Israel election as Netanyahu's bloc falls short of majority
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Israel's election has produced no clear winner, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party emerging as the largest single party in the Knesset but his right-wing bloc falling short of a governing majority. Israelis surged to the polls at a turnout of more than 77%, and partial results give Netanyahu's bloc 54 seats in the 120-seat parliament, while the opposition alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot holds 49 seats. Both leaders have already begun intense political wrangling to form a coalition, but analysts caution the picture could shift because the early count was skewed toward areas with strong right-wing support and a high number of absentee ballots, mainly from soldiers, remain uncounted; final results are not expected for another day or two.

Addressing supporters overnight, Netanyahu stopped short of declaring victory but said the right-wing bloc had "a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public, among the Jewish public and all those who support the Jewish state." He added: "We must form a strong, national, right-wing government. That is what must be done." Eisenkot struck a different tone, declaring, "The public has chosen change. The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust. The Israeli public voted against Benjamin Netanyahu continuing as prime minister." He pledged to work with partners to translate "the people's decision into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israel's citizens."

The projected record performance of Israel's Arab-led parties has added a volatile element to the coalition arithmetic. Arab Israelis, who often identify as Palestinian citizens of Israel and represent one-fifth of the population, appeared to turn out in unprecedented numbers, with the Joint List and Ra'am projected to win a combined 17 seats. According to the latest partial results, a partnership between Eisenkot's bloc and the Arab parties would yield 66 seats — enough to unseat Netanyahu. But Netanyahu has ruled out partnering with Arab-majority lists, citing a lack of shared values, and most Jewish opposition parties made the same pledge during the campaign. "Probably the most important phenomenon of this election is the rise and the revival of the Arab vote," said Daniel Shek, a former Israeli ambassador. Honaida Ghanam, of the Palestinian Forum for Israeli Studies, called the exclusion a "veto rooted in a racist structure that regards the Arab citizen as illegitimate and as an unwanted partner." Mansour Abbas, leader of Ra'am, said politicians "say one thing before elections and speak a different language after elections," noting his party had previously joined the diverse coalition that temporarily unseated Netanyahu between 2021 and 2022.

The election underscores deep divisions in Israeli society and has served as both a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership and a vote on the country's direction. Netanyahu faces a corruption trial on charges he denies, and his current coalition partners have taken Israel on a hardline religious and nationalist trajectory over the past four years, including a judicial overhaul plan that drew mass protests before the unprecedented Hamas-led attacks on 7 October 2023, which triggered wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Despite those turbulent events, voting patterns changed little. "The relative weight of the two main sides: pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu is about the same," pollster Tamar Hermann said before the election. "People expected that after October 7th, Netanyahu will be down the drain or even toppled but it didn't happen."

The next steps are now prescribed by Israel's fragmented political system. After the final results are presented to President Isaac Herzog next week, he will consult leaders of all elected parties and ask the candidate deemed most likely to assemble a coalition to do so. That candidate will have a maximum of six weeks to secure a 61-seat majority; if they fail, others may be allowed to try. If no one succeeds, a new election will be held within months and the process repeated. In the meantime, Netanyahu's government remains in a caretaker role without authority to enact major policy changes. Veteran Israeli journalist Yaakov Katz described the coming negotiations as "all these different political kinds of wizardry," adding that it "could take weeks or months to see if someone is actually capable of forming a government."

stories.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after fleeing Brazil following election loss
body: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right Brazilian senator who lost Sunday's presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, landed in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday morning after fleeing Brazil in a journey that took him through Argentina and Ecuador. He arrived at the Miami-Opa Locka executive airport with his wife and two daughters and left under police escort without speaking to reporters.

Argentina's migration directorate said Bolsonaro and his family crossed the border by land late Tuesday via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge in Misiones province, "with valid travel documentation and without any legal impediment to entering the country." They boarded a private Gulfstream jet at Puerto Iguazú airport at about 11:30pm bound for Guayaquil, Ecuador, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace, before continuing to Miami. In Miami, the family, shielded by black umbrellas, climbed into a dark gray Ford Expedition MAX and sped away under police escort; Bolsonaro is expected to hold a press conference Wednesday or Thursday. The US State Department said it would grant visas to Bolsonaro and his family, and President Donald Trump said he would approve the move, calling them "fine people" and repeating his criticism of the election: "The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible." He also said the extension of voting times was a "very bad look."

Bolsonaro's departure came despite a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports in connection with a money-laundering investigation in which he denies wrongdoing. He had refused to concede defeat, pledged to challenge the results, and was due to lose his immunity from prosecution in February when his term in the Senate ends. According to the AFP news agency, he also holds Italian citizenship, allowing him to travel even after his Brazilian and diplomatic passports were canceled. On Monday, he had written on Instagram that he had no intention of leaving the country and would "hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."

Lula, marking his 81st birthday at an event in Brasília, called the flight "shameful." "This is what the family Bolsonaro are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as he's become accustomed to doing," he said. "I keep imagining what's on the conscience of a citizen who just lost the elections and flees his country … He who owes nothing, fears nothing. A citizen who sneaks out of his country owes something. The act of leaving Brazil is shameful." Lawmakers from Lula's Workers' Party asked the Supreme Court to order Bolsonaro's arrest.

Bolsonaro is the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is imprisoned on charges of leading a conspiracy to remain in power after his 2022 defeat. The elder Bolsonaro spent three months in Florida after that election and later spent two nights at the Hungarian embassy in Brasília while facing trial over the attempted coup; while under house arrest after a 27-year prison sentence, he attempted to destroy his electronic ankle monitor with a soldering iron. Flávio Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida could deepen a rift between the United States and Brazil: during the campaign, Lula accused the Trump administration of colluding with the Bolsonaro family to help them return to power, and Trump has previously alleged that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. About a dozen politicians and influencers aligned with the elder Bolsonaro have fled Brazil in recent years.

Bolsonaro is under investigation in at least two criminal cases, including one examining suspicions that he was involved in a money-laundering scheme worth about £680m ($905m) involving betting companies. Shortly after the election result, Brazilian police asked the Supreme Court to retain his passport, citing a podcast interview last Friday in which his brother, former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, said that if his brother lost, he should not concede and should go to the US. Reports said the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case of defeat, organized mainly by Eduardo, who lives in self-imposed exile in the US and lobbies the Trump administration against Lula, with the plan "organized and enabled by a lawyer close to the Bolsonaro clan." Brazilian federal police face criticism for failing to prevent the departure, and some in the government suspected allies had planted reports that he was already en route to the US to distract from his real plan to go through Argentina. There remains a gap between the last time Bolsonaro was seen by allies, about 6pm Monday, and his entry into Argentina late Tuesday; it is unclear how or when he reached the border, and he had disappeared from public view for more than 24 hours. The aircraft he boarded had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since early Tuesday, when reports first emerged that he intended to flee, and the Argentinian newspaper Página/12 reported that it belonged to businessman Sergio Daniel Mastropietro, who was investigated in a scandal involving the alleged payment of bribes linked to medicine purchases for people with disabilities.

stories.headline: Zelensky says Ukraine recaptured territory in secret pipeline and air assault operations
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine's battlefield position is the strongest it has been in some time after his forces recaptured territory through a series of offensives, including a previously undisclosed operation that used underground gas pipelines to outflank Russian positions near Kupiansk in the northeastern Kharkiv region.

In his nightly video address, Zelensky cited a report by senior commanders to say that the "Veles" operation, conducted near Kupiansk, marked the first time Ukrainian troops used gas pipelines in the northeast. "It is a strong operation, well planned and technology-driven. The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to advance past our positions," he said. "Our fighters turned this tactic against the Russians and used the underground infrastructure against the occupiers with extraordinary success."

Zelensky also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the "Vivaldi" operation further north, aimed at preventing Russian advances in key areas. In the Vivaldi offensive, one senior commander reported last month that Ukraine's Third Army Corps had cleared an area of 75 square kilometres (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 square kilometres, focusing on the north of the "fortress belt" cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk in the Donbas, whose capture would bring Russia closer to seizing the entire region.

His remarks came as Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare direct phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, lasting around 90 minutes on Tuesday, before holding a separate conversation with Zelensky. The call, which Kyiv says it was involved in planning, drew criticism from other European leaders opposed to direct engagement with Putin. Støre defended the call as an effort to ensure Putin heard European views as well as those from the US, saying he did not think Putin would change his mind "but he gets to hear our position very clearly. I am worried that some of these messages do not reach him when the Americans talk to him." The Kremlin showed no softening, insisting that any lasting peace must "unconditionally" take Russia's interests into account, while Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov dismissed the call as part of the "information war," saying European countries were seeking a role in the negotiation process.

Asked whether peace could come without Ukraine ceding territory, Støre said: "Today Russia controls nearly 20 per cent (of Ukrainian territory). Ukraine will never sign a deal that recognises that they have lost territory, but whether they can take the current frontline as a reality and as a starting point, that is a different question." He said the big question was what security guarantees Ukraine could receive after a peace deal, noting Putin "recognises that this is the big question." Støre also said Norway was keen to introduce de-escalation steps such as stopping attacks on energy infrastructure, halting strikes on ships exporting Ukrainian grain, and conducting prisoner-of-war exchanges.

In other developments, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said the information war around Ukraine would continue and likely escalate; Ukrainian drones struck the Azot chemical plant in Novomoskovsk, Tula Oblast, with unverified videos showing smoke from a fire; a Russian drone strike on Kharkiv injured five people, including a 4-year-old child; and Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region in two weeks, with air defence package deliveries delayed. A UN-backed inquiry reported Monday that Russia committed war crimes and crimes against humanity by intentionally attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, and found evidence that Russia recruited men from 29 countries through deception or coercion, mostly from vulnerable and marginalized communities. Russia's largest lender Sberbank said a Ukrainian drone attack on its data centre in the Saratov region did not cause abnormal cash outflows.

stories.headline: Fed expected to hold rates steady at October meeting ahead of midterms
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters, AP
body: The Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at the conclusion of its two-day policy meeting on Wednesday, even as inflation accelerates, according to surveys of market participants and economists. Investors put the chance of a pause at about 90%, based on CME Group’s FedWatch Tool, while CNBC’s latest Fed Survey of 30 fund managers, strategists and economists found that 93% expect no rate hike this week. The decision comes less than a week before the midterm elections, which have focused heavily on concerns about the cost of living.

The Fed’s benchmark interest rate currently stands between 3.75% and 4%, a level that marks a significant drop from a recent peak in 2023 but remains well above the near-zero rate set at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. The central bank raised its key rate last month for the first time in three years, from about 3.6% to 3.9%. Inflation rose to a four-month high in September, with the Consumer Price Index increasing 3.7% from a year earlier, more than a percentage point above the Fed’s 2% target, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Fuel prices climbed in response to unrest in the Middle East, and the U.S. crude oil benchmark is forecast to be at $88 a barrel six months from now, up from $82 in the September survey but below the current level of $101.

Despite the pause expected this week, 76% of respondents in the CNBC survey anticipate a rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December, and more than half expect the central bank to hike next year by an average of about two rate increases. The odds of a quarter-point rate hike in December are pegged at 75%, according to the FedWatch Tool. At least two Fed voters are expected to dissent from the decision to keep rates unchanged, the CNBC survey found. A plurality of 40% of respondents said the Fed must slow growth below potential to solve the inflation problem, while 27% said the Fed does not need to slow the economy and 23% said it needs to slow it only somewhat.

The economic picture is complicated by a weak jobs report: employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp slowdown from the 162,000 added in August and well below economists’ expectations. The unemployment rate is forecast to remain steady at 4.2% through the remainder of the year but rise to 4.4% in 2027. Respondents in the CNBC survey put the risk of a U.S. recession in the next year at 26%, down from 29% in the prior survey. The outlook for the S&P 500 stayed stable for this year at around 7,600 but moved down to 8,033 for next year from 8,274 in the prior survey. The index closed at 7,676 Monday.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized the Fed for raising interest rates, including a social media post hours after last month’s hike that said: “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed, faces a host of challenges, including that some drivers of inflation — such as the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — will not easily be tamed by higher interest rates. The congressional election is also seen as a market risk: 63% of CNBC survey respondents said there is some market risk from legal challenges that could extend uncertainty over which party controls Congress. More than half of respondents said the most likely outcome is Democratic control of both houses, up from 29% in the last survey.

The Fed’s rate decision may also draw attention to the challenge posed by inflation, a top issue among voters. In a memo to clients, Deutsche Bank Research said the upcoming midterms could factor into a potential decision to hold rates steady, though the election would not be a “primary consideration.” The memo added: “We could imagine that all else equal the Fed might prefer to stay out of the headlines for raising rates just ahead of a midterm election where affordability is the principal concern.” Fed Chair Warsh is expected to hold a news conference at 2:30 p.m. EDT on Wednesday to discuss the decision.

stories.headline: Microsoft Q1 Earnings Preview: Azure Growth, AI Spending in Focus
body: Microsoft (MSFT) is set to report fiscal first-quarter earnings after the bell Wednesday, with Wall Street focused on growth in its Azure cloud business and the financial impact of its massive artificial-intelligence build-out. The report comes two days after the company announced it is offering buyouts to up to 60,000 eligible employees as part of cost-cutting efforts tied to its AI investments.

Analysts surveyed by Bloomberg expect earnings per share of $4.27 on revenue of $90.6 billion, up from $4.13 per share and $77.6 billion in revenue in the same period last year. The quarter is the first under Microsoft’s new segment structure, which replaces the previous three-segment model with two: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. Agents and Infra, which includes Azure, Microsoft 365 cloud services, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions, and frontier and support services, is expected to generate the most attention. Revenue for that segment is forecast to rise 22.5% to $75.6 billion, with Azure contributing $32.2 billion and Microsoft 365 adding $27.4 billion. Devices and Consumer, encompassing search and advertising, Xbox, and Windows OEM and devices, is projected to decline 6% to $15 billion.

Capital expenditures, including leases, are expected to top $45.9 billion in the quarter, more than double the $19.3 billion Microsoft spent in Q1 last year, underscoring the scale of its AI infrastructure push. Remaining performance obligations (RPO)—contracts Microsoft has booked but not yet recognized as revenue—are projected to reach $705.6 billion, up 77% from $389 billion a year earlier, signaling strong future demand.

Microsoft stock drifted lower in premarket trading Wednesday ahead of the report. The shares lagged for most of fiscal 2026 but rallied about 35% since July after the company’s fiscal fourth-quarter results. Investors will be looking for updates on Azure and Copilot growth as Microsoft continues to expand its AI services. The earnings release will also provide the first look at how the new segment structure affects financial reporting and investor analysis.

stories.headline: Vertiv blowout earnings signal accelerating AI infrastructure buildout
body: Vertiv Holdings, a key provider of data center infrastructure and a partner of Nvidia, surged on Wednesday after reporting third-quarter earnings that far exceeded expectations. Shares of Vertiv (VRT) rose 15% in morning trading to around $240, according to MarketSurge, as the company's results sent an upbeat signal about the pace of the artificial intelligence buildout ahead of major Big Tech earnings reports.

The company reported adjusted earnings of $2.21 per share for the third quarter, a 78% increase from the same period a year earlier. The strong sales beat affirms that the AI infrastructure buildout is accelerating, according to MarketWatch, and helped Vertiv shrug off broader industry concerns about the AI investment cycle.

The earnings beat comes as investors await results from the largest technology companies, and it provides an early, concrete signal that demand for AI-related infrastructure remains strong. The stock's double-digit gain on Wednesday reflected investor relief and optimism that the buildout phase of the AI cycle is still accelerating, not slowing.

stories.headline: Spanish cup matches suspended after Madrid train crash kills 68
body: All 24 matches in the Spanish Copa del Rey scheduled for Wednesday have been suspended as a mark of respect after at least 68 people were killed in a train crash near Madrid. The Spanish FA (RFEF) announced the decision in a statement, saying it was made in solidarity with the victims. More than 500 passengers were travelling on the trains when they collided and derailed in the province of Toledo.

Five top-flight teams—Levante, Alaves, Valencia, Celta Vigo and Real Betis—were due to play in the first-round matches on Wednesday. Spanish giants including Real Madrid, Barcelona and Atletico Madrid are not scheduled to enter the competition until the last-32 round.

Barcelona expressed its "deepest condolences" to the victims on social media, offering support and solidarity to the families and friends of those affected and wishing a speedy recovery to the injured. Real Madrid issued a statement on its website expressing "deepest sorrow" over the accident, extending condolences to the families of the deceased and offering "full support" to the emergency services and all those involved in the rescue efforts.
Thursday's matches remain unaffected for now. The RFEF has not yet released a revised schedule for the postponed Wednesday games.

stories.headline: Colts trade Buckner, Nelson in NFL deadline fire sale; Taylor could be next
body: The Indianapolis Colts set off the NFL trade deadline season Tuesday, Oct. 27, shipping defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers and guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks within hours of each other — and attention immediately turned to whether running back Jonathan Taylor will be next before the Nov. 10 deadline.

The Colts sent Buckner, 32, back to the team that selected him seventh overall in the 2016 draft, receiving a 2027 fourth-round pick in return. Seattle, meanwhile, acquired Nelson, an eight-time Pro Bowler and six-time All-Pro, for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Both players are in the final year of their contracts and can become free agents after this season.

Analysts across outlets read the moves as the start of a full rebuild. The Colts fired general manager Chris Ballard after a disappointing start, and they are rebuilding without a first-round pick. NFL.com wrote that Indianapolis needs "as many lotto tickets as possible for the next general manager" and expected Ed Dodds to listen to offers on pending free agents and "potentially others under contract beyond 2027." Grades were mostly strong for the buyers — FOX Sports gave the 49ers a B+ and Seahawks an A, while NFL.com gave the 49ers an A- and Seahawks an A — but mixed for the Colts, who received a C+ and B+ for the Buckner deal and a B+ and B for the Nelson trade. Some analysts said Indianapolis might have gotten more by waiting closer to the deadline, though the fourth-round pick for Buckner was still seen as better than a possible 2028 compensatory fifth-rounder.

Buckner, who had grown vocal about the Colts' mounting losses, gives San Francisco an interior boost after the 49ers' pass rush managed a league-low 20 sacks last season and only 15 this year. He had four sacks, eight quarterback hits and 31 total tackles in seven games, and his 47 sacks since 2020 are tied for second among defensive tackles behind Chris Jones. NFL.com noted signs of decline, however: his pressure rate is down to 8.3% this season from 10.3% in 2025 and 11.7% in 2024, and his run-stop rate has dipped to 12.4%. Paired with Osa Odighizuwa — and eventually with Nick Bosa, who is expected back from a calf injury — Buckner should bolster a defensive line for a team in a Super Bowl window.

stories.headline: Rays force World Series Game 5 with 12-inning walk-off win over Brewers
body: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Pinch-hitter Ben Williamson singled home the winning run in the bottom of the 12th inning, and the Tampa Bay Rays staved off World Series elimination with a 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday night, forcing a Game 5. The Rays, who trailed 3-2 entering the bottom of the 12th after Milwaukee rookie Cooper Pratt hit a tiebreaking solo homer off Ian Seymour, rallied after a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz on Junior Caminero's leadoff grounder. Liam Hicks singled, and Jonny DeLuca's single to center drove in pinch-runner Cedric Mullins to tie the score. Chandler Simpson's single loaded the bases, and Williamson — who had been 1 for 15 in the postseason — hit a chopper over first baseman Jake Bauers and into right field to end the game.

Pratt, a 22-year-old rookie who also tied the score at 1 with an RBI double in the second, became the first rookie to hit an extra-inning homer in the World Series. David Hamilton had earlier homered for Milwaukee, and Jackson Chourio collected a single and double, improving to 10 for 20 in the Series. The Brewers had won eight straight games and were bidding to become only the second team to sweep a League Championship Series and the World Series. Tampa Bay ended that streak in front of a crowd of 40,514 at Tropicana Field, where many Brewers fans waved yellow towels and some wore cheeseheads.

Tampa Bay became just the fifth of 26 teams that fell behind 3-0 in the World Series to win Game 4; the previous four all lost Game 5. Of 43 teams to trail 3-0 in any best-of-seven postseason matchup, the only one to rebound and win the series was the Boston Red Sox against the New York Yankees in the 2004 American League Championship Series. The Rays, seeking their first championship, will try to extend the series again in Game 5 on Wednesday night at Tropicana Field.

The game also carried broader significance beyond the diamond. The New York Post noted that the thriller served as a reminder of what baseball fans will be missing once the season ends, as a lockout by owners is considered almost certain when the current collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1. For now, the Rays have ensured at least one more day of baseball.

stories.headline: Eagles' Hurts recovering after playing with life-threatening blood clot
body: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season after multiple blood clots were found in his lungs, a life-threatening condition if not treated quickly. The 28-year-old played a full game hours after being diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in his calf during the team's visit to London earlier this month, raising questions about the NFL's handling of player health and safety.

Hurts first reported an issue to the team on 8 October, after another player stepped on his left calf during a game on 4 October. He trained in full and received treatment. On 10 October, the day the Eagles arrived in London, Hurts visited the Cleveland Clinic, where an ultrasound showed a superficial blood clot (vein thrombosis) in his calf. He was cleared to play. Hurts returned to the team hotel at about 3am on 11 October and played the full game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. A follow-up ultrasound was recommended within 72 hours, and he was cleared for the flight home that evening.

On 14 October, after daily treatment, a second ultrasound showed the clot had moved, and Hurts was ruled out of the next game. A joint statement on 19 October said further tests revealed deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli—multiple blood clots in both lungs. His treatment involves blood-thinning medicine, and he is expected to make a full recovery but will miss the remainder of the season.

Dr. Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, who was in London that weekend and arranged for Hurts to be evaluated at the Cleveland Clinic, said the league does not have a protocol for such situations. He stated that those who dealt with Hurts were "incredibly conservative" and that he had "complete confidence" in how the Eagles handled the matter. The NFL Players Association (NFLPA) initially called for a full investigation, noting the NFL had said it did not plan to review the care Hurts received. However, the league and NFLPA later released a joint statement saying they are "working together to review the matter."

The case has drawn scrutiny to the NFL's approach to player health during its growing international schedule, which includes a record nine games this year. Dr. Niko Mihic, the local medical coordinator for the NFL's next international game in Madrid on 8 November, told BBC Sport that blood clots among athletes are "not that common" and that decisions on whether to allow a player to sleep, stay active, or fly long-haul involve medical judgment on a case-by-case basis. "It's not as simple as some people think," he said. "There's an amount of judgement that goes into this."

Hurts is expected to make a full recovery, but Dr. Mihic noted that "the worst risk factor for recurrent embolisms is having had one previously." The Eagles, who have lost five straight games and lack an experienced backup quarterback, face a challenging season. With the trade deadline two weeks away, the team that reached two of the past four Super Bowls could be facing a rebuild.

stories.headline: Lilly's retatrutide beats Ozempic in head-to-head diabetes trial
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Eli Lilly announced Wednesday that its investigational drug retatrutide outperformed Novo Nordisk's Ozempic in a large Phase 3 clinical trial of adults with type 2 diabetes. In the head-to-head study, patients on the highest dose of retatrutide achieved a 2.2 percentage-point reduction in blood sugar (A1c) after 80 weeks, compared with a 1.8 percentage-point reduction for those on Ozempic. The results, based on participants who stayed on treatment, also showed that those on the highest dose of retatrutide lost 20.9% of their weight, while those on Ozempic lost 9.4%.

In absolute terms, patients on the 9 mg dose of retatrutide lost an average of 44.3 pounds, and those on the 12 mg dose lost 47.4 pounds, versus 20.9 pounds for the highest Ozempic dose (2 mg). The drug also provided better heart benefits, including improvements in cholesterol and blood pressure. Retatrutide is a once-weekly injection that mimics three hunger-regulating hormones: GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon. By contrast, Ozempic and Wegovy (also from Novo Nordisk) mimic only GLP-1, while Lilly's own Mounjaro and Zepbound mimic GLP-1 and GIP. The addition of glucagon, a hormone that promotes fat burning even at rest, is what sets retatrutide apart.

Lilly said it plans to submit retatrutide for approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in early 2027. The drug is not yet FDA approved, and the FDA has warned that any versions consumers have obtained online come from the black market and should not be used. Novo Nordisk also has an experimental drug, CagriSema, which expects FDA approval by the end of the year. Neither CagriSema nor retatrutide is currently approved. Ozempic and Mounjaro are FDA-approved to treat type 2 diabetes, while Wegovy and Zepbound are approved for weight management. As with any prescription medication, individuals should consult a health care provider about whether these drugs may be appropriate for them.

stories.headline: Epic's market dominance stifles health tech innovation, investigation finds
body: A STAT investigation has found that Epic Systems Corp., the nation's dominant seller of electronic health records, relies on fierce and uncompromising business tactics that have crushed competitors, thwarted innovation, and put a single, privately-held company in charge of patient data needed to power medicine's next generation of technology. Epic collects more than $6.5 billion a year in revenue, wins the lion's share of new contracts, and holds health information on some 8 in 10 Americans.

The investigation found that Epic selectively withholds access to patient data to the disadvantage of rival software tools, leaving its own products unchallenged. That practice has put one company in charge of determining who thrives and who withers in the market for health technology innovation, and hospital executives along with app developers say Epic's growing market power is blocking adoption of the most beneficial software products.

Executives of 12 companies that Epic showcases on its app marketplace for hospital customers told STAT that the software giant has undercut their businesses by denying access to crucial data interfaces and technical specifications, spreading negative rumors about their products, or charging high fees for access. Epic's data systems are used by a majority of large U.S. health systems.

Epic says it provides more connections to its data than required by federal law and has won praise for its support of its many hospital customers. But the company's record-keeping systems, invented at the dawn of personal computers in a Wisconsin basement, are now so ubiquitous inside the nation's largest hospitals that almost nothing happens in this technology universe without Epic's involvement — or approval.
STAT is seeking input from people with direct knowledge of Epic's business practices to further examine how the company's actions may affect hospitals' technology choices and innovation.

stories.headline: FDA and CMS unveil steps to speed personalized gene therapies for rare diseases
body: The Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday published draft guidance that would streamline approval of individualized gene therapies, while the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced plans to expand a model aimed at increasing patient access to these treatments. The coordinated actions, announced by the Department of Health and Human Services, are intended to accelerate development and access for patients with rare diseases, including those with ultra-rare conditions for which no treatment currently exists.

The FDA draft guidance outlines a framework for allowing a single biologics license application (BLA) to cover multiple patient-specific variants of a gene therapy. Central to the framework is the Individualized Feature Space (IFS), a set of pre-defined criteria describing how a therapy can vary between patients—for example, those whose disease is caused by different genetic mutations—while remaining within the scope of one BLA. According to the FDA and CMS, when a new patient-specific variant falls within those boundaries and assays show adequate safety and activity, sponsors can submit it to the BLA without needing to perform additional clinical trials. The guidance also addresses manufacturing, safety testing, and labeling.

The CMS component involves broadening the Cell and Gene Therapy (CGT) Access Model, a voluntary initiative launched in January 2024 under which CMS negotiates outcomes-based agreements on behalf of state Medicaid programs. The model initially focused on gene therapies for sickle cell disease; in December 2024, Vertex Pharmaceuticals and bluebird bio—developers of Casgevy and Lyfgenia, respectively—joined the program. CMS said it will release a Request for Applications in the coming months to broaden the model's scope, enable negotiations to begin sooner after FDA approval, and welcome applications for therapies already approved or licensed.

The actions follow other recent FDA initiatives, including the Plausible Mechanism Pathway announced in November 2025 by former Commissioner Marty Makary and former CBER director Vinay Prasad, which was intended to expedite therapies for exceedingly small patient populations where randomized trials are not feasible. The draft guidance also comes less than two weeks after the FDA debuted its Rare Disease Framework Initiative, designed to standardize the agency's approach to scientific evidence and bring rare disease therapies to patients faster.

Reaction to the announcements was positive among rare disease advocates and analysts. Paul Scribner, vice president of community programs and education at the PKD Foundation, said of the draft guidance at a rare disease event on Tuesday, "It's sort of putting a flag in the ground and saying, 'This is important.'" RBC Capital Markets analysts, attending the National Organization for Rare Diseases Breakthrough Summit in Washington, D.C., wrote in a note to investors that they came away "incrementally more positive on the rare disease regulatory setup," citing a constructive tone from FDA officials and a strong desire to harmonize regulatory standards. The analysts also noted that multiple congressional staffers at the summit expressed bipartisan support for clinical trial reform for rare disease, with U.S. midterm elections less than a week away.

stories.headline: Artiva Biotherapeutics shuts down after trial failure and two patient deaths
body: San Diego-based Artiva Biotherapeutics said Tuesday it is winding down after abandoning its lead immunotherapy candidate, AlloNK, for rheumatoid arthritis and laying off about 94% of its workforce. The decision follows updated clinical data showing the off-the-shelf natural killer cell therapy was initially effective but that the durability of the response did not meet the company's threshold to support continued development. The company also faced scrutiny after two patients in its clinical trials died, though neither death appeared to be related to the AlloNK therapy itself.

Artiva, founded in 2019, had 115 full-time employees in June and planned to grow, according to federal filings. The layoffs will affect nearly all staff, many of whom work at the company's headquarters at 5505 Morehouse Drive in San Diego. An official WARN notice detailing the layoffs has not yet been filed. The company said it is exploring alternatives to maximize shareholder value, including a possible sale, merger, or liquidation. “We don't have a specific timeline that we can share at this point. AlloNK was the only program we were developing, and now that we are no longer continuing development, we are exploring alternatives that maximize shareholder value,” said Noopur Batsha Liffick, head of investor relations.

The two patient deaths were assessed by an investigator and an independent safety review board. In one case, a Phase 2a trial participant suffered a fatal neurological event, leukoencephalopathy, following treatment. The investigator determined the death was likely related to fludarabine, a mild chemotherapy regimen typically administered before cell therapy to lower white blood cell counts and make room for the new cells, rather than to the cell therapy itself. In the second case, a participant died suddenly approximately two months after initiating treatment.
